title: Mythos attack on 3rd-round PQC algorithm candidate puts it out of commission
gist: Anthropic's Mythos security model, driven by a researcher with no cryptography expertise using roughly 60 hours and $100,000 of compute, halved the effective key strength of HAWK—a third-round NIST post-quantum signature candidate—prompting its developer to withdraw it, and separately cut the input requirement for a meet-in-the-middle attack on weakened AES from about 2^105 to 2^89. The results are incremental and lab-bound, but they mark the first time an AI system materially altered a live cryptographic standards process.

themes.theme: HAWK's withdrawal from the NIST PQC process

insights.claim: HAWK, a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme that had survived two full rounds of NIST evaluation, was withdrawn by its own developer one day after Anthropic published the Mythos findings.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: An AI system has now directly removed a candidate from a national cryptographic standards process—a concrete, verifiable capability milestone rather than a benchmark score.
insights.locator: Following Anthropic’s Monday announcement of the results

insights.claim: HAWK was specifically in a third round of testing designed to catch exactly the class of flaw that Mythos found, meaning the AI beat the human adversarial-review process at its own stated purpose.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: If AI outperforms multi-year human peer review inside its designed scope, standards timelines and confidence intervals for cryptographic migration need rewriting.
insights.locator: HAWK was in a third round of testing

insights.claim: The weakness can be mitigated by doubling HAWK's key size, but the added computation makes it less desirable than already-available PQC signing algorithms such as ML-DSA and FN-DSA.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Cryptographic competition is decided on performance-at-security-level, so a 2x key inflation is commercially fatal even when the scheme is not literally broken.
insights.locator: The weakness can be mitigated by doubling the key size

insights.claim: Google PQC expert Sophie Schmieg said HAWK was already suspected to have weaknesses that would eventually be found, and concluded the paper finishes it off.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Expert priors were already negative on HAWK—tempering how much novel capability the Mythos result actually demonstrates.
insights.quote: Basically with this paper, HAWK is dead
insights.locator: Sophie Schmieg, an expert in PQC at Google

themes.theme: Cost and skill economics of AI-assisted cryptanalysis

insights.claim: The HAWK attack took about 60 hours of work and roughly $100,000 of compute, executed by an Anthropic researcher with no expertise in cryptography.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A six-figure compute bill and zero domain expertise is a price point any state actor or well-funded firm can clear—expertise ceases to be the scarce input in cryptanalysis.
insights.locator: With about 60 hours of work and about $100,000 of compute cost

insights.claim: Mythos worked semi-autonomously in an agentic harness with only occasional human guidance and nontechnical direction, conducting literature review, mathematical reasoning, and computational experiments before building its own end-to-end verification pipeline.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Self-verification is the piece that makes autonomous research outputs trustworthy enough to act on—watch it as the gating capability for AI in regulated technical domains.
insights.quote: To find the attack, Claude Mythos Preview worked semi-autonomously in an agentic harness, with occasional human guidance and nontechnical direction.
insights.locator: Anthropic elaborated

insights.claim: The improved method emerged from two separate agents working largely independently, where one initially rejected the approach as unworkable and the second found a way to make it work before they converged.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Multi-agent disagreement-then-convergence is being used as a research method, not just an engineering pattern—an architectural signal for how frontier labs are scaling reasoning.
insights.locator: To find the improved method, Mythos deployed two separate agents

insights.claim: Mythos currently remains available only to a select group of trusted users, so the capability is deliberately not broadly distributed.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Gated release of offensive-capable models is the emerging norm—creates an access asymmetry that is itself a competitive and geopolitical variable.
insights.locator: Anthropic said its Mythos model

themes.theme: Recombination, not invention, as the AI edge

insights.claim: Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green argued the attack is concerning precisely because it invents no new mathematics—it recombines well-known tools that were lying around, which is the kind of work AI is especially suited to.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Reframes AI research risk: the exposed surface is every field with a large unexploited combinatorial space of existing techniques, not just fields awaiting genius.
insights.quote: What’s particularly concerning (and so especially ripe for AI) is that the attack does not invent fundamentally new mathematics,
insights.locator: Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor

insights.claim: HAWK's security rests on the hardness of the Lattice Isomorphism Problem, and the best classical attack works by finding automorphism symmetries; Mythos output a previously unknown method for finding such symmetries, halving the key length.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The mechanism is specific and checkable, which is why the community accepted the result within a day—contrast with unfalsifiable AI capability claims.
insights.locator: The math HAWK’s security relies on

themes.theme: The AES result and its limits

insights.claim: Mythos found a new meet-in-the-middle technique using a Möbius Bridge fingerprinting algorithm that cut required plaintext inputs against a weakened AES from roughly 2^105 to 2^89, which Anthropic says reduces attack time 200- to 800-fold.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A concrete order-of-magnitude improvement against the world's most deployed cipher—still infeasible, but the direction of travel matters for long-horizon data-retention risk.
insights.locator: Mythos helped to find a new meet-in-the-middle technique

insights.claim: The AES test used a weakened seven-round variant whereas specification-compliant AES uses 10, 12, or 14 rounds depending on key size, so the real speed-up against production AES is unknown.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The gap between challenge instances and production parameters is where AI cryptanalysis claims should be discounted hardest.
insights.locator: Further, the actual speed-up is unknown

insights.claim: Even producing 2^89 plaintext inputs is beyond reach outside a laboratory, so neither attack threatens any deployed cryptosystem today.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: No near-term operational risk—positioning around 'crypto is broken' headlines is premature.
insights.locator: The ability to produce that many inputs

themes.theme: Skepticism and what was conspicuously absent

insights.claim: Anthropic did not report whether Mythos was aimed at more mature and heavily tested cryptosystems such as elliptic curve cryptography and RSA, where improvements would be far more impressive.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The omission is the tell: absence of results against the hardest, most-studied targets suggests the demonstrated edge is narrower than the framing implies.
insights.locator: Not mentioned in Anthropic’s report

insights.claim: Because the most impressive result came against an algorithm still in its infancy, there is no way to know whether conventional human cryptanalysts were already close to the same attack.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Counterfactual attribution is the unresolvable weak point of all AI-research-capability claims—demand controlled comparisons before repricing anything.
insights.locator: By achieving the most impressive result against an algorithm

insights.claim: The cryptosystems tested were weakened 'challenge instances' supplied by specification authors for adversarial peer review, a standard practice, but the production versions are considerably more robust.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Provides the standard discount factor to apply to any cryptanalysis headline: challenge-instance results are not production results.
insights.locator: Second, the cryptosystems tested were weakened versions

insights.claim: Vendors of AI security platforms have a vested interest in exaggerating benefits and AI-assisted cryptanalysis remains untested, yet evidence is growing that LLMs offer significant advantages in finding cryptographic weaknesses.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The balanced read: do not underwrite the marketing, but do not assume the capability curve stalls either—position for optionality, not certainty.
insights.quote: AI-assisted cryptanalysis remains untested, and providers of these platforms have a vested interest in exaggerating their benefits.
insights.locator: Ultimately, the lesson from the research is simple

insights.claim: Anthropic states the cybersecurity community already cannot keep up with the volume of bugs language models discover, because human triage, verification, and remediation processes were not designed for that throughput.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Creates immediate demand for automated triage, verification, and patch-orchestration tooling—the bottleneck moves downstream of discovery.
insights.quote: The cybersecurity community is now grappling with the fact that language models are able to discover so many bugs that the standard human processes (like vulnerability triage, verification, and remediation) struggle to keep up,
insights.locator: The Monday blog post goes on to argue

insights.claim: Anthropic predicts academic cryptography research will hit the same wall, with human researchers becoming the bottleneck on validating autonomously produced novel results for validity, novelty, and utility.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: If validation becomes the scarce resource across scientific fields, verification infrastructure and formal-methods tooling become the chokepoint worth owning.
insights.quote: As language models increasingly produce novel research outputs autonomously, human researchers may become bottlenecked on studying and validating these results for technical validity, novelty, and utility.
insights.locator: We predict that the same will soon be true

insights.claim: The outcomes are explicitly incremental—they reduce the work needed to defeat systems rather than breaking anything, and the underlying mathematical primitives remain safe for now.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Frames the correct time horizon: this is a slope change in cryptanalytic productivity, not a discrete break event.
insights.locator: First, the outcomes are incremental
